title: Diversity made the best products. AI is threatening both.
excerpt: Diverse teams built the best products. AI adoption inequality is quietly threatening the conditions that make that possible, and the people who made those teams great are the ones being left behind.
lead: Diverse teams built the best products. AI adoption is now quietly dismantling the conditions that made that possible, and the people who made those teams great are the ones being left behind.
lead_sub: The distilled version of a conversation with Chelsea Karaolis, co-founder of Unify, about who gets left behind as AI accelerates, and what to do about it.
next_title: AI has broken the B2B FinTech pricing playbook. The replacement is not obvious.

title: Architecture is a commercial decision
excerpt: Architecture is treated as a technical decision. It is a commercial one. What a CEO should expect is a CTO who can explain it in those terms, and a CPO who makes sure they do.
lead: I sat in a room of senior product leaders while someone presented on architecture. When the speaker asked who felt confident they understood the commercial implications of their own architectural choices, most hands stayed down.
lead_sub: These were the people whose job is to hold the commercial picture of the product.
next_title: AI has broken the B2B FinTech pricing playbook. The replacement is not obvious.

title: AI has broken the B2B FinTech pricing playbook. The replacement is not obvious.
excerpt: Satya Nadella called SaaS dead in December 2024. Most people heard a technology claim. It was a commercial one, and once you see it that way, the implication for every B2B FinTech business is immediate.
lead: AI did not just change what software can do. It broke the pricing model underneath it.
lead_sub: SaaS was never a technology. It was always a commercial model.

lead: AI has made building software cheap. So cheap you can throw code away and rebuild it.

title: You raised a Series C. Your product team is still operating at Series A.
excerpt: The scaling crack that almost nobody names before it breaks — and the five transitions that separate Series A operating habits from Series C expectations.
lead: I walked into a company and was given a list of commitments already made to the board. When I sat with the team delivering them, two things became clear: they weren't sure what they'd committed to, and nobody had defined what success looked like.
